Currency pair.long:
A currency pair is the quotation of one currency against another — EURUSD is euros priced in US dollars. Buying the pair buys the first currency and sells the second simultaneously; there is no such thing as buying a currency in isolation.

This two-sided structure is the feature that separates FX from most other trading. Every position is a relative bet: long EURUSD profits if the euro strengthens against the dollar, whether that happens because Europe improves or America deteriorates. A trader with a correct view on the euro can still lose because the dollar moved more. Analysis therefore has to cover two economies, two central banks and two interest rates per trade.

The pair's price states how much of the quote currency one unit of the base currency buys — EURUSD at 1.10 means one euro buys 1.10 dollars.

Where people get fooled: reading a pair as a single asset going up or down. A EURUSD rally during broad dollar weakness says nothing about the euro — every dollar pair rallied. Checking the counter-currency's behaviour across other pairs is the difference between a view and an accident.
Currency pair.usage: Generally the unit of all FX trading; every position is long one currency and short another at once.

Base / quote currency.long:
In a currency pair the base is the first currency and the quote is the second: in AUDUSD, the Australian dollar is the base and the US dollar the quote. The price says how many units of quote one unit of base buys.

The convention matters mechanically. Position sizes are expressed in base currency units — a standard lot is 100,000 of the base — while profit and loss accrues in the quote currency, converted to your account currency at prevailing rates. A pip's dollar value therefore depends on which side of the pair your account currency sits, and on the pair's current price for crosses. Getting this arithmetic wrong is the most common sizing error in retail FX, and it silently changes the risk per trade.

Quotation direction is convention, not economics — the euro is conventionally a base, the yen conventionally a quote — so a rising USDJPY means a weaker yen, while a rising EURUSD means a weaker dollar.

Where people get fooled: pip-value assumptions. A pip on EURUSD is worth a fixed amount in dollars, but a pip on EURGBP is worth a variable amount in dollars, and an account denominated in Australian dollars adds a second conversion. Sizing rules built on one pair's arithmetic quietly misprice risk on the next.
Base / quote currency.usage: Typically needed for sizing: lots are counted in base currency, P&L lands in quote currency, and the conversion to your account adds a step.

Pipette.long:
A pipette is a tenth of a pip — the fifth decimal place on most pairs, the third on yen pairs — introduced when brokers moved to fractional pricing to advertise tighter spreads.

A pip itself is the conventional minimum quote increment: the fourth decimal on most pairs, the second on yen pairs. Pipettes subdivide it, so a EURUSD quote of 1.10432 is 1.1043 and 2 pipettes. The finer grid genuinely allows tighter spreads to be shown and filled, but its main practical effect is on reading quotes and calculating: a trader who miscounts the decimal by one place sizes a position ten times too large or too small, and platform tickets showing 43 points may mean 4.3 pips depending on the vendor's vocabulary.

Points, pips and pipettes are used inconsistently across platforms, which is the real trap — the words are broker-specific, the decimals are not.

Where people get fooled: spread marketing. A spread advertised as 2 sounds tight until it turns out to be 2 pips on a platform whose competitor quotes 12 pipettes for the same width. Comparing costs requires converting everything to one unit, and the ambiguity is not accidental.
Pipette.usage: Generally the fifth decimal on non-yen pairs; check whether a platform's numbers mean pips or pipettes before sizing anything.

Majors / minors / exotics.long:
The majors are the heavily traded dollar pairs — EURUSD, USDJPY, GBPUSD, USDCHF, AUDUSD, USDCAD, NZDUSD. Minors, or crosses, pair major currencies without the dollar, such as EURGBP or AUDJPY. Exotics pair a major with an emerging-market or small-economy currency — USDTRY, USDZAR, EURPLN.

The classification is really a liquidity gradient, and costs follow it. Majors carry the tightest spreads because dealer competition is fiercest there; crosses cost more; exotics cost multiples more, with spreads that widen dramatically in stress. Exotics also carry risks the majors mostly do not: overnight swap rates that can dwarf price movement, gap-prone reactions to local politics, and occasional convertibility or intervention surprises — documented pegs have broken with moves that jumped straight through every resting stop.

For most purposes the majors contain the tradable opportunity set; the exotics contain mostly cost and event risk dressed as volatility.

Where people get fooled: exotic volatility looks like opportunity. The daily ranges are wide, but the spread consumes a proportionally larger share of every trade, the swaps bleed holding positions, and the occasional gap through a stop returns years of small wins. Ranges are advertised; the cost structure is not.
Majors / minors / exotics.usage: Generally a liquidity and cost tiering: majors cheapest and deepest, exotics wide, swap-heavy and gap-prone.

Carry trade.long:
A carry trade borrows a low-interest-rate currency to hold a high-interest-rate one, collecting the rate differential daily through swap credits. Long AUDJPY when Australian rates far exceed Japanese rates is the retail-accessible classic.

The income is real and arrives on schedule, which is what makes the trade seductive. The risk arrives on no schedule at all: carry pairs accumulate crowded positioning precisely because the income attracts leverage, and when risk appetite breaks, everyone exits the same door at once. The resulting unwinds are abrupt and deep — carry returns are famously described as picking up pennies in front of a steamroller, with documented episodes (the 2008 yen crosses among them) erasing years of accumulated interest in weeks.

The distribution matters more than the average: many small positive days, rare large negative ones. Strategies with that shape systematically look better in short backtests than they are.

Where people get fooled: the daily credit reads as an edge with no downside visible in recent data. The downside is real, large and clustered; it simply has not happened lately, and the calm period during which the income compounds is exactly when the position size drifts upward toward the eventual unwind.
Carry trade.usage: Generally held for the interest differential via swap credits; the return profile is steady income punctuated by rare violent unwinds.

Swap / rollover fee.long:
The swap, or rollover, is the interest adjustment applied to FX positions held past the daily cut-off — usually 5pm New York. It reflects the interest-rate difference between the two currencies: hold the higher-yielding side and you may be credited; hold the lower-yielding side and you are debited.

The mechanics have retail-specific teeth. Brokers add a margin to the interbank rate, so the debit you pay is worse and the credit you receive smaller than the raw differential. Wednesday's rollover is typically tripled to account for the weekend's settlement. On exotic pairs the swap can be large enough to dominate the trade's economics entirely — a position held for weeks can lose on swap while winning on price.

For multi-day trading, swap belongs in the cost model next to spread and commission, and for carry-style positions it is the entire thesis, so the broker's specific rates — published on every platform, rarely read — are worth checking rather than assuming.

Where people get fooled: swing traders who cost their strategy at spread only. A system holding positions five nights a week pays or earns swap five times per trade, and on the wrong side of a wide differential the quiet nightly debit converts a marginally profitable price strategy into a losing account.
Swap / rollover fee.usage: Typically charged or credited nightly on held FX positions; a real cost line that belongs in any multi-day strategy's arithmetic.

Interbank market.long:
The interbank market is the top tier of FX: major banks dealing directly with each other and through electronic venues, where the prices every retail quote descends from are actually made.

FX has no central exchange. It is a decentralised dealer network, with the deepest liquidity concentrated among a handful of banks and the primary venues they trade on. Prices cascade outward from there: prime brokers extend access to funds, liquidity aggregators repackage bank feeds, and retail brokers assemble their quotes from those feeds with their own spread added. Your chart is a downstream copy — usually faithful on majors in calm conditions, and diverging most exactly when it matters, during news spikes and thin hours, because each broker's aggregation and filtering differs.

This structure explains several retail experiences: quotes differing between brokers, spreads blowing out at 5pm New York or in the Asian lull, and stop levels that printed on one feed but not another.

Where people get fooled: treating their broker's feed as the market. Disputing a stop-out with a chart from a different broker misunderstands the plumbing — there is no single official price in FX, only a network of dealer quotes, and your contract is with your counterparty's version of it.
Interbank market.usage: Generally the source of all FX pricing; retail quotes are downstream copies with broker-specific spread and filtering applied.

Dealing desk / B-book.long:
A dealing-desk or B-book broker takes the other side of client trades internally rather than passing them to the market. The client's loss is the broker's revenue; the client's win is the broker's cost.

The practice is legal, regulated and near-universal in retail FX and CFDs, and it is less lurid than it sounds: because most retail accounts lose over time, holding the aggregate book is reliably profitable without any need to rig individual trades. Brokers typically run hybrid models — internalising most flow, hedging or A-booking the clients who win consistently. Published regulator data in several jurisdictions has repeatedly shown a substantial majority of retail CFD accounts losing money, which is the statistical foundation the model rests on.

The conflict of interest is structural rather than operational: the broker profits from client losses in aggregate, which shapes incentives around leverage marketing, bonus offers and re-quotes even where execution is clean.

Where people get fooled: imagining the desk hunts their individual stops. It rarely needs to — the aggregate book does the work. The practical response is not paranoia but structure: regulated venue, transparent execution statistics, and position sizes that survive the spread widening every broker applies at the worst moments.
Dealing desk / B-book.usage: Generally the internalising model of retail FX/CFD brokers; profitable because the aggregate client book loses, not because individual trades are rigged.

ECN broker.long:
An ECN broker routes client orders into an electronic communication network where they interact with quotes from banks, funds and other clients, charging a commission instead of widening the spread. The model is marketed as the honest alternative to the dealing desk.

The genuine differences: raw spreads plus explicit commission, direct market interaction, and no structural profit from client losses. The marketing gap: the label is unregulated in most places, so brokers describe hybrid or entirely internalised models as ECN freely. Genuine ECN execution shows its nature in the details — variable raw spreads that occasionally touch zero, commission on every ticket, depth-of-book data, and slippage in both directions rather than only against you.

Whether the model is cheaper depends on arithmetic, not virtue: raw spread plus commission on an ECN account versus the all-in spread of a standard account, measured on the pairs and sessions you actually trade.

Where people get fooled: the label doing the diligence. An unverifiable ECN badge on a website is a marketing asset, and some of the worst-regulated brokers wear it loudest. Execution statistics, regulatory registration and the observable spread behaviour are the checkable facts; the acronym is not one.
ECN broker.usage: Typically means commission-plus-raw-spread execution into a network; the label is unregulated, so verify with execution behaviour rather than branding.

Requote.long:
A requote is a broker's response to an order stating the requested price is no longer available and offering a new one to accept or decline. It appears at the moments prices move fastest — news releases, session opens, thin liquidity.

Some requoting reflects reality: prices genuinely change between click and server, and a dealing-desk broker quoting a price it must honour has an incentive to re-confirm when the market has moved. But the pattern of requotes is diagnostic. Symmetric ones — sometimes better for you, sometimes worse — suggest honest latency. Requotes that only ever appear when the move favours you, on a platform that fills instantly when the move favours the broker, describe an execution model tilted by design.

Market-execution platforms replaced most requoting with slippage: the order fills at the available price, whatever it is. That trades the annoyance of rejection for the risk of a worse fill, which at least shows up honestly in the statistics.

Where people get fooled: accepting requotes reflexively during volatility, which converts every fast market into systematically worse entries. If a strategy depends on news-time execution, requote behaviour is not an annoyance but a cost line — and often the line that decides the strategy does not survive retail plumbing.
Requote.usage: Generally a dealing-desk phenomenon in fast markets; its symmetry, or lack of it, is a readable signal about the broker's execution model.

Fixing.long:
A fixing is a scheduled benchmark rate set at a specific time — the dominant one being the WM/Reuters London 4pm fix — used to value portfolios, settle contracts and translate corporate flows. Enormous volume concentrates into the fixing window because so many participants are contractually tied to its price.

That concentration creates predictable mechanics: order flow builds into the window, and price frequently moves toward the fix and fades after it. It also created one of FX's largest documented scandals — in 2013-14, investigations found dealers at major banks colluding to push fixes in favourable directions, resulting in billions in fines and criminal charges. The episode is worth knowing not for outrage but for calibration: manipulation happens where mechanical flows meet discretion, and it was caught at the top of the market, not the bottom.

For a retail trader the fix mostly matters as a timing hazard: spreads and volatility behave strangely around 4pm London, and end-of-month fixes are the strangest.

Where people get fooled: reading fix-window moves as information. A surge into 4pm London on month-end is usually rebalancing flow with no view attached, and it reverses precisely because nobody holding it had one. Trading the aftermath as a breakout mistakes plumbing for conviction.
Fixing.usage: Generally the London 4pm benchmark window; mechanically driven flow, odd spreads, and documented historical manipulation make it a time to know about.

NDF.long:
A non-deliverable forward is a forward contract on a currency that cannot be freely delivered offshore — typically emerging-market currencies with capital controls, like the Indian rupee or Korean won. At maturity, no currency changes hands; the contract cash-settles in dollars against the difference between the agreed rate and the prevailing fix.

NDFs exist because controls prevent ordinary offshore forwards, so an offshore market grew that references the currency without touching it. Pricing embeds not just interest differentials but the market's view of control risk, devaluation risk and offshore dollar demand — which is why NDF-implied rates can diverge sharply from onshore rates for the same currency and date. That divergence is itself information about stress.

Retail traders meet NDF economics mostly indirectly: exotic-pair CFDs on controlled currencies are priced off NDF curves, inheriting their wide spreads, heavy carry and event risk.

Where people get fooled: treating a controlled currency's chart like a free one. The price is a negotiated offshore approximation shaped by policy risk, its spreads and swaps are hostile, and a control change or peg adjustment moves it discontinuously — through any stop, at a price no chart predicted the day before.
NDF.usage: Generally the offshore cash-settled instrument for controlled currencies; retail exposure arrives via exotic CFDs priced from NDF curves.

Triangular relationship.long:
The triangular relationship ties three pairs together arithmetically: EURUSD multiplied by USDJPY must equal EURJPY, and every cross is similarly the product of its dollar legs. If the relationship broke, riskless profit would exist by trading the triangle, so high-speed arbitrage keeps it locked within transaction costs.

For a retail trader this is not an opportunity — the arbitrage decays in microseconds and belongs to colocated firms — but it is a genuinely useful lens. It means crosses are derived prices: EURJPY's movement decomposes exactly into its euro leg and its yen leg, and reading which leg is driving explains the move. A EURJPY rally on a day every yen pair rallied is a yen event wearing a euro costume.

The relationship also disciplines analysis: a view on a cross is implicitly a view on two dollar pairs, and if those views contradict your other positions, the portfolio is arguing with itself.

Where people get fooled: analysing a cross as an independent instrument and doubling exposure by accident. Long EURJPY and long USDJPY is substantially one yen-short position sized twice, and the correlation that merges them shows up exactly when both lose together.
Triangular relationship.usage: Generally used to decompose cross moves into their dollar legs and to spot accidental doubled exposure; the arbitrage itself is not retail-accessible.

FX session overlap.long:
FX trades continuously through the week, but its liquidity follows the sun through three sessions — Asia, London, New York — and the overlaps are where volume concentrates. The London-New York overlap is the deepest stretch of the day; the London open and the New York morning bracket most of the day's range on the major pairs.

The pattern is structural, not folklore: dealers, funds and corporate flow work business hours, so participation genuinely doubles when two centres are open together. Spreads tighten in the overlaps and widen in the gaps — the late New York afternoon and the pre-Tokyo lull are notoriously thin, and the 5pm New York rollover minutes produce spread spikes on even the majors.

From Perth, the geography is workable: London opens mid-afternoon AWST, and the London-New York overlap runs through the late evening, so the deepest liquidity of the day falls in accessible hours rather than the middle of the night.

Where people get fooled: backtesting on daily bars and trading in the thin hours. A strategy validated on liquid-session data pays double or triple spread executing in the lull, and stop placement calibrated to overlap volatility sits inside the noise of the rollover spike. When you trade is a cost parameter, not a preference.
FX session overlap.usage: Generally the map of when FX is cheap and deep to trade; overlaps tighten spreads, gaps and rollover minutes widen them.
